  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S3.SS3" title="In 3 Practical Mechanisms for Neural Weight Generation: A Standardized Taxonomy ‣ Position: Weight Space Should Be a First-Class Generative AI Modality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">3.3 </span>Generative Predictors for Weight Synthesis</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_subsection">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" title="In 3.3 Generative Predictors for Weight Synthesis ‣ 3 Practical Mechanisms for Neural Weight Generation: A Standardized Taxonomy ‣ Position: Weight Space Should Be a First-Class Generative AI Modality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Hypernetworks (fastest, best for personalization).</span></a></li>

</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_subsection"><a href="#S3.SS4" title="In 3 Practical Mechanisms for Neural Weight Generation: A Standardized Taxonomy ‣ Position: Weight Space Should Be a First-Class Generative AI Modality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">3.4 </span>Training Strategies and Collapse Avoidance</span></a>
<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_subsection">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1" title="In 3.4 Training Strategies and Collapse Avoidance ‣ 3 Practical Mechanisms for Neural Weight Generation: A Standardized Taxonomy ‣ Position: Weight Space Should Be a First-Class Generative AI Modality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Augmentation and regularization.</span></a></li>

</ol></li>

<ol class="ltx_toclist ltx_toclist_subsection">
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_paragraph"><a href="#S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1" title="In 3.5 Evaluation Metrics: Beyond One Simple Accuracy ‣ 3 Practical Mechanisms for Neural Weight Generation: A Standardized Taxonomy ‣ Position: Weight Space Should Be a First-Class Generative AI Modality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title">Three-Axis Framework.</span></a></li>

</ol></li>
</ol></li>
<li class="ltx_tocentry ltx_tocentry_section"><a href="#S4" title="In Position: Weight Space Should Be a First-Class Generative AI Modality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_title"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_ref">4 </span>Applications Enabled by Weight Generators</span></a>

<article class="ltx_document">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Position: Weight Space Should Be a First-Class Generative AI Modality</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Zhangyang Wang
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>University of Texas at Austin
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Peihao Wang
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>University of Texas at Austin
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Kai Wang
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Tencent Hy
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author"><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Correspondence to: </span><a href="mailto:atlaswang@utexas.edu">atlaswang@utexas.edu</a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Neural network checkpoints have quietly become a large-scale data
resource: millions of trained weight vectors now exist, each encoding
task-, domain-, and architecture-specific knowledge.
This position paper argues that <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">model checkpoints should be treated as a
first-class data modality, and that generative modeling in weight space
should be standardized as a core machine learning primitive</span>.
Recent advances demonstrate that neural weights
can be synthesized on demand, often matching fine-tuning performance
while reducing adaptation cost by orders of magnitude.
We contend that these results reflect an underlying structural fact:
high-performing models occupy low-dimensional, highly structured regions
of weight space shaped by symmetry, flatness, modularity, and shared
subspaces.
Building on this view, we organize existing methods into a five-stage pipeline, survey
applications where the approach is already practical, and clarify current
limits: adapter-scale and conditional generation are advancing rapidly,
while unrestricted frontier-scale checkpoint synthesis remains open. Our goal is to shift the community’s default mindset from optimizing
models per task to sampling models from learned weight distributions, accelerating toward an era in which <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">AI systems
routinely improve or create other AI systems</span>.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction and Statement of Position</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">The success of generative AI has so far been asymmetric: we can
<em id="S1.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_upright">generate</em> pixels, waveforms, and tokens on demand, but we still
<em id="S1.p1.1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_upright">construct</em> - via repeated, costly optimization - the models that
perform this generation.</span>
This asymmetry increasingly defines the bottleneck of modern machine
learning.
Training a single foundation model can emit as much
<math id="S1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{CO}_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>CO</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{CO}_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> as a small airline fleet <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Patterson et al., 2021</a>)</cite>,
while even modest fine-tuning remains prohibitive for many start-ups,
academic groups, and edge deployments.
At the same time, demand for
<em id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">ultra-rapid</em>, <em id="S1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">task-specialized</em>, and
<em id="S1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">user-personalized</em> models is accelerating—from on-device copilots
to adaptive robotics to personalized healthcare.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We argue that progress is throttled less by hardware than by
<em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">methodological inertia</em>.
Neural network parameters are still treated as immutable artifacts to
be rediscovered from scratch for every new task or user.
Yet a century of statistics
teaches a different lesson: when data exhibit structure, we should
<em id="S1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">model and sample</em> that structure rather than repeatedly re-optimizing it.
Recent results indicate that trained neural weights themselves form such
a structured data modality.
HyperNetworks generate full convolutional weight tensors in a single
forward pass <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ha et al., 2017</a>)</cite>;
graph-conditioned predictors initialize unseen architectures without
task-specific training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al., 2021</a>)</cite>;
diffusion models denoise checkpoints in weight space to yield
ImageNet-ready ConvNeXt backbones <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
More recently, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> demonstrates that even large language models (LLMs) can be adapted by
<em id="S1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">directly generating</em> low-rank weight updates in seconds,
often matching or exceeding fine-tuning performance.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.18632v1/figure1_weightgen_regime_map.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/246;" width="452" height="246"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
A regime map for weight-space generation (see $3). We frame neural weight generation as conditional sampling from <math id="S1.F1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(W\mid A,C,R)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>W</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(W\mid A,C,R)</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S1.F1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> denotes generated weights or weight updates, <math id="S1.F1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> specifies the architecture graph and tensor schema, <math id="S1.F1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> encodes task or user conditions, and <math id="S1.F1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> captures training-recipe and checkpoint-lineage information. The three regimes distinguish whether architecture and conditioning are fixed or varied: checkpoint-level generation under fixed settings, condition-driven generation for adapters or personalization, and graph-conditioned generation across architectures. This view separates the placement problem, handled naturally by graph or schema encoders, from the value-generation problem, handled by diffusion, hypernetwork, or flow decoders.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Position.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We posit that <span id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold ltx_font_italic">neural network checkpoints constitute a
first-class data modality, and that generative modeling in weight space
should be standardized as a core machine learning primitive.</span>
Under this view, model creation is reframed as
<em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">conditional sampling</em>: given a task description, data domain,
user context, or architectural specification, one samples from a learned
distribution of high-performing weights. Crucially, this position does <em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">not</em> claim that weight generation
solves all problems of training or scalability.
Nor is it reducible to the connectedness of minima
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Entezari et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Garipov et al., 2018</a>)</cite>:
connectivity guarantees that paths exist, but it does not explain how to
reliably reach flat, robust, calibrated, or domain-adapted regions.
Achieving those properties requires learning an explicit,
conditioned density over weight configurations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Why Now?</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Weight-space generation is no longer a speculative idea; it is enabled
by a concrete shift in the ML ecosystem.
Open-science efforts have produced an unprecedented corpus of trained
models:
(i) the Hugging Face Hub alone hosts over one million public checkpoints
across modalities;
(ii) TensorFlow Hub, ONNX Model Zoo, and open releases from major
industrial labs further expand this repository;
(iii) recent academic studies explicitly treat neural weights as data,
including large-scale analyses of tens of thousands of trained models;
(iv) parameter-efficient fine-tuning has exploded the number of
<em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">task-conditioned</em> checkpoints, with over 22 000 LoRA adapters for
the LLaMA family alone as of 2025.
Together, these trends provide both the <em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">data substrate</em> and the
<em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">deployment pressure</em> that make generative modeling in weight space
timely and actionable.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Contributions.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper advances the position through four concrete contributions:</p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theory.</span>
We synthesize decades of optimization theory and empirical results, to explain why generative modeling of weights is
both feasible and non-trivial.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Framework.</span>
We formulate weight-space generation as conditional sampling
<math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(W\mid A,C,R)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>W</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(W\mid A,C,R)</annotation></semantics></math> (Fig <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction and Statement of Position ‣ Position: Weight Space Should Be a First-Class Generative AI Modality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), distinguishing fixed-architecture generation,
condition-driven adaptation, and cross-architecture generation, and
relate these regimes to a five-stage pipeline:
tokenization <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> embedding <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> generative
predictor <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> training strategy <math id="S1.I1.i2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> evaluation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Evidence.</span>
We survey demonstrated applications, while separating
practical current regimes from still-open frontier-scale full
checkpoint generation.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Agenda.</span>
We analyze alternative views, failure modes, and
concrete steps toward this new paradigm.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">By elevating weights from optimization artifacts to generative objects,
we aim to shift the community’s default question from
<em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">“How do we fine-tune this model?”</em> to
<em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.2.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">“What distribution of models should we sample from?”</em></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Theoretical Foundation of Weight Space Geometry:
Why Feasible, Yet Non-Trivial</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If neural network weights are to be treated as a <em id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">generative
modality</em>, then any successful generator must respect the intrinsic
geometry of weight space itself.
This section synthesizes what decades of optimization theory and recent
empirical studies reveal about that geometry, and explains how they both <em id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">enable</em> and <em id="S2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">constrain</em> weight
generation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Far from forming a random high-dimensional cloud</span>, the set of
high-performing neural networks concentrates on structured subsets of
parameter space.
These structures explain why learned generative models can empirically succeed.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Mode Connectivity of Solutions</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Partly because of over-parameterization, many trained neural networks do not behave as isolated optima in the raw parameter space. While naive linear interpolation between independently trained models
often incurs large loss barriers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shevchenko and Mondelli, 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kuditipudi et al., 2019</a>)</cite>,
empirical results revealed <em id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">mode connectivity</em>:
continuous low-loss paths linking solutions trained from different
initializations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Garipov et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Draxler et al., 2018</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Theoretical work clarifies when such connectivity arises.
Solutions exhibiting dropout or noise stability admit barrier-free
connections in ReLU networks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kuditipudi et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, and
sufficiently wide networks provably admit near-zero-loss paths between
SGD solutions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shevchenko and Mondelli, 2020</a>)</cite>.
Even moderately over-parameterized architectures, such as CIFAR-10
ResNets, empirically exhibit this phenomenon <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Garipov et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Draxler et al., 2018</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Connectivity provides evidence that many low-training-loss SGD solutions are not isolated in parameter space. It does not by itself prove that all well-generalizing solutions form a single manifold.
Furthermore, this result alone does <em id="S2.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">not</em> make weight generation
trivial.
Connectivity guarantees that <em id="S2.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">paths</em> exist, but offers no mechanism
for <em id="S2.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">sampling</em> points with desired properties such as robustness,
calibration, or transferability.
For generation, the challenge is hence not reachability, but
<em id="S2.SS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">density modeling</em> (see $2.4): reachability between trained points is often possible, but sampling robust, calibrated, transferable, or safe models still requires learning a structured conditional density.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Permutation Symmetries and Quotient Geometry</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A central reason for the apparent multiplicity of minima is parameter
symmetry <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goodfellow et al., 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Choromanska et al., 2015</a>)</cite>.
Permuting hidden units or channels preserves the network’s function
while producing numerically distinct weight vectors.
As a result, each functional solution corresponds to an equivalence
class in raw parameter space, creating flat directions and degenerate
minima.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Interpolation between unaligned solutions introduces artificial loss
barriers due to mismatched neuron identities.
When permutation symmetry is explicitly factored out, these barriers
vanish.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Entezari et al., 2022</a>)</cite> conjectured that, modulo permutation, SGD
solutions occupy a single basin.
<span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Git Re-Basin</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ainsworth et al., 2023</a>)</cite> provided constructive
evidence, demonstrating zero-barrier linear connectivity after neuron
alignment.
Related symmetry-aware matching improves model averaging and federated
learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yurochkin et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tatro et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For generative modeling, this implies that the natural object of study
is not raw weight space <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbb{R}^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>n</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbb{R}^{n}</annotation></semantics></math>, but a <em id="S2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">quotient space</em> under
symmetry.
Generators that ignore this structure waste capacity modeling redundant
degrees of freedom.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Flatness and Low Intrinsic Dimension</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond symmetry, trained solutions occupy remarkably flat regions of
the loss landscape.
Hessian analyses show that only a small number of eigenvalues are large
at SGD minima, with most directions exhibiting near-zero
curvature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sagun et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib76" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ghorbani et al., 2019</a>)</cite>.
Perturbations along flat directions often leave performance
unchanged. Flatness correlates strongly with generalization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2020</a>)</cite>,
and invariant measures confirm that broader basins generalize better
despite reparameterization issues <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dinh et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Petzka et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.
Methods that explicitly promote flatness, such as Sharpness-Aware
Minimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib77" title="" class="ltx_ref">Foret et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, consistently improve performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Multiple lines of evidence indicate that the <em id="S2.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">effective</em> dimension of optimization trajectories and searchable subspaces can be far smaller than the ambient parameter count.
Lottery Ticket and subspace training results show that networks can be
trained successfully within low-dimensional affine
subspaces <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Frankle and Carbin, 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib75" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jaiswal et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Large-scale training dynamics reveal that SGD trajectories
explore a tiny, low-rank subspace of parameter space
regardless of initialization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gur-Ari et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, though not without caveat whether a single dominant subspace really exists <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Recent memory-efficient optimizer designs  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhu et al., 2025</a>)</cite> explicitly exploit this phenomenon: see <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">Balzano et al., 2025</a>)</cite> for more reviews. These results imply that high-performing weights occupy
a <em id="S2.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">thin, structured manifold</em>.
Sampling must therefore capture strong inter-parameter correlations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4 </span>Implicit Bias: Why Solution Density Is Not Uniform</h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Optimizers exhibit strong implicit bias toward solutions with
specific geometric properties. This is critical for weight generation:
the target distribution is <em id="S2.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">highly non-uniform</em>.
Effective generators must learn to model this density.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In deep linear and homogeneous networks, gradient descent with weight
decay provably minimizes effective rank over training
trajectories <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib78" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ji and Telgarsky, 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib79" title="" class="ltx_ref">Le and Jegelka, 2022</a>)</cite>.
More broadly, SGD combined with common regularizers implicitly performs
rank minimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib80" title="" class="ltx_ref">Galanti et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, explaining the low effective
rank observed. When data lie on a low-dimensional manifold, optimal solutions align
with that intrinsic structure <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib81" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ongie et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">As another example, SGD also favors small-norm, max-margin solutions in classification
settings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib82" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soudry et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib83" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lyu and Li, 2020</a>)</cite>.
Although theory for nonlinear networks remains incomplete, empirical
evidence consistently shows that optimization concentrates probability
mass in a small subset of geometrically regular solutions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.5 </span>Compositionality and Modularity</h3>

<div id="S2.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Neural networks frequently internalize compositional structure when
trained on structured data.
Empirical studies show that modern networks decompose into coherent
sub-circuits corresponding to reusable functions or
concepts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Csordás et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qiu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>,
with individual blocks exhibiting interpretable roles
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bau et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. Recent theoretical and empirical work suggests that gradient-based
training induces latent modular representations within weight
space <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cranmer et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang and Wang, 2025</a>)</cite>.
Network morphisms such as Net2Net <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2016</a>)</cite>
and progressive stacking <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gong et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2022</a>)</cite>
explicitly exploit this modularity.
Model editing and merging <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wortsman et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> further
demonstrate empirically that specific skills correspond to localized parameter
subsets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For generation, modularity explains both promise and difficulty.
On one hand, generators can recombine learned modules to generalize
across tasks.
On the other, module boundaries are not smooth or spatially local in
raw parameter coordinates, complicating naive notions of locality and
requiring structured tokenization and curriculum strategies.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.6 </span>Shared Representations and Universal Subspaces?</h3>

<div id="S2.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Despite architectural diversity and/or training data or task differences, trained networks often converge toward
remarkably similar internal representations. The <em id="S2.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Platonic representation hypothesis</em> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huh et al., 2024</a>)</cite> was the first to
posit that high-performing models recover a common structure dictated
by the data-generating process rather than architectural details. More evidence includes linear alignment of representations across models
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kornblith et al., 2019</a>)</cite> snd successful model stitching
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bansal et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.
Recent large-scale empirical studies suggest the existence of
shared low-dimensional subspaces that capture variation across datasets, initializations, tasks
and architectures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaushik et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Although still preliminary, this discovery has the potential to explain the success of transfer learning,
distillation, and adapter-based methods.
It also suggests that generators potentially need not learn
architecture-specific distributions from scratch, but can operate in
shared latent coordinates that instantiate across architectures.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS6.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Summary.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Taken together,
neural weight space is structured and low-dimensional, biased by
optimization, making weight generation <em id="S2.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">feasible</em>.
At the same time, the absence of smooth locality, the presence of
symmetry, and the non-uniform density make the problem
fundamentally non-trivial.
Any successful generator must therefore be symmetry-aware,
bias-aligned, and capable of capturing long-range correlations rather
than naive smoothness.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Practical Mechanisms for Neural Weight Generation: A Standardized Taxonomy</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Armed with the geometric insights of Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Theoretical Foundation of Weight Space Geometry: Why Feasible, Yet Non-Trivial ‣ Position: Weight Space Should Be a First-Class Generative AI Modality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we now
turn to the practical question: <em id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">how can we learn a model that
samples from the structured and low-dimensional
distribution of high-performing neural weights?</em>
Contemporary systems increasingly converge on a modular pipeline that
mirrors the workflow of modern generative AI for images and text, but
with crucial differences: weights exhibit strong permutation symmetries, weak “spatial locality” in raw
coordinates, and heavy-tailed inter-layer dependencies.
As a result, each stage of the pipeline must be re-designed to encode
the right invariances and to avoid degenerate solutions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we synthesize the rapidly growing literature into a standardized,
five-stage blueprint: <span id="S3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">tokenization</span>,
<span id="S3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">embedding</span>, <span id="S3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">generative predictor</span>, <span id="S3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">training
strategy</span>, and <span id="S3.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">evaluation</span>.
Our goal is <em id="S3.p2.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">mechanistic</em>: to explain how each
design choice operationalizes the geometry of Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Theoretical Foundation of Weight Space Geometry: Why Feasible, Yet Non-Trivial ‣ Position: Weight Space Should Be a First-Class Generative AI Modality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>,
and to highlight which choices appear most practical today.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Regimes and scope.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To avoid overstating feasibility, we separate three regimes that recur
throughout this section:
(i) <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">adapter generation</em> (e.g., LoRA-like low-rank updates),
(ii) <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">mid-scale full-weight generation</em> (e.g., 10M–200M parameter
vision backbones), and
(iii) <em id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">cross-architecture generalization</em> (predicting weights for
unseen graphs).
The field is currently most mature in (i) and increasingly competitive
in (ii), while (iii) remains an open frontier.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As depicted in Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction and Statement of Position ‣ Position: Weight Space Should Be a First-Class Generative AI Modality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, a useful unifying abstraction is the conditional family <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p(W\mid A,C,R)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>W</mi><mo fence="true" lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∣</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p(W\mid A,C,R)</annotation></semantics></math>,
where <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W</annotation></semantics></math> denotes weights or weight updates, <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the architecture graph and tensor schema, <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> denotes task, domain, prompt, dataset, or user condition, and <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> denotes training recipe and quality metadata<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            In practice, <math id="footnote1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> need not be a user-facing input: a user may specify only <math id="footnote1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>, while the generator marginalizes over, selects, or internally conditions on suitable recipe and quality factors.</span></span></span>. When <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> is fixed, the parameter slots are known and the generator mainly models values. When <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math> varies, the generator performs conditional adaptation over a known layout. When <math id="S3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="A" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>A</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">A</annotation></semantics></math> varies, the generator must also map generated tensors back to operator types, shapes, and connectivity. In this sense, graph encoders mainly solve the placement problem, while diffusion, flow, or hypernetwork modules solve the value-generation problem.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Tokenization of Weights: What Is “Local”?</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tokenization maps heterogeneous parameter tensors into a common
“language” suitable for sequence, set, or graph models. Yet one must confront a key concern:
<em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">weight space lacks obvious locality</em>.
Unlike pixels or tokens, raw weights do not live on a natural grid.
Instead, locality is <em id="S3.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">architectural</em>: weights incident to the same
neuron/channel are coupled; kernels share spatial structure; attention
blocks couple across layers through residual streams; and symmetries
introduce many equivalent coordinate representations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We therefore view tokenization as choosing an <em id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">inductive bias for
dependency structure</em>.
Three families dominate practice: see next. We believe the practical trend is toward <em id="S3.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">hybrid locality</em>: preserve intra-layer
structure via chunking and tags, while learning inter-layer dependencies
via sequence models, recurrence, or diffusion refinements.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">(1) Flattening and chunking (sequence view).</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A naive approach flattens all parameters into one long vector, but this
destroys layer structure and aggravates symmetry.
Early hypernetwork-based NAS (e.g., SMASH <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brock et al., 2018</a>)</cite>)
used coarse flattening, while subsequent work emphasized
structured partitions and function-preserving transformations such as
Net2Net <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2016</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Modern large-scale generators partition weights into coherent tokens.
RPG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> slices each layer into fixed-length chunks, applies per-layer
normalization, and appends positional tags (layer index, chunk index) to
break permutation ambiguity across tokens.
SANE similarly operates on thousands of tokens, but encodes them into
learned embeddings rather than directly modeling raw floats
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
This “token-with-position” paradigm implements a weak form of locality:
it assumes that chunks within a layer are more correlated than chunks
across layers, while still permitting the generator to learn global
dependencies through attention or recurrence.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">(2) Set encodings (permutation-invariant view).</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Permutation symmetry ($ <a href="#S2" title="2 Theoretical Foundation of Weight Space Geometry: Why Feasible, Yet Non-Trivial ‣ Position: Weight Space Should Be a First-Class Generative AI Modality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) suggests representing
collections of neurons/channels as <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">unordered sets</em>.
Set encoders and permutation-invariant pooling attempt to quotient out
label symmetries at the representation level.
For example, Set-Based Neural Network Encoding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Andreis et al., 2024</a>)</cite>
treats layer parameters as sets of neuron vectors and uses
permutation-invariant operations to form representations.
Such tokenization can reduce spurious variation, but may
fail to model long-range inter-layer correlations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A practical lesson from <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Git Re-Basin</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ainsworth et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and
related alignment work is that <em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">symmetry can be handled either
before modeling (canonicalization / alignment) or inside the model
(permutation-invariant encoders)</em>.
Most current generators choose the latter implicitly (via tags,
invariances, and data augmentation), because perfect canonicalization is
itself a hard problem.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">(3) Graph tokenization (architecture-as-graph view).</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When architectures vary, tokenization naturally becomes graph-structured.
Graph HyperNetworks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al., 2021</a>)</cite> treat the network as a DAG
<math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})</annotation></semantics></math>, with node attributes encoding
layer types and shapes; message passing propagates context and produces a
weight prediction per node.
Graph MetaNetworks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lim et al., 2024</a>)</cite> extend this idea to diverse
architectures, aiming to predict parameters for unseen graphs.
Graph tokenization is the clearest path toward regime (iii), but its
ability to scale to modern foundation models is still limited by memory
and by the difficulty of capturing dense long-range dependencies.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Embedding and Latent Representation Design</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Embedding compresses tokenized weights (and conditions) into latent
variables that make generation tractable.
This stage operationalizes two geometric facts from
Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Theoretical Foundation of Weight Space Geometry: Why Feasible, Yet Non-Trivial ‣ Position: Weight Space Should Be a First-Class Generative AI Modality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>:
(i) good solutions lie on a thin manifold, and
(ii) the density on that manifold is highly non-uniform.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Autoencoding and layer-wise balancing.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Early work showed that simple weight statistics predict performance
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Unterthiner et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.
Hyper-Representations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2022</a>)</cite> learn an autoencoder over
entire networks, and emphasize <em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">layer-wise loss normalization</em> so
small layers are not ignored.
SANE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>)</cite> produces layer-wise latents from large
token sequences, enabling scalable encoding of large networks. Later, diffusion-style approaches often use an explicit encoder-decoder pair
<math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E:\mathbb{R}^{d}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{d^{\prime}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup><mo rspace="0.108em" stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>′</mo></msup></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E:\mathbb{R}^{d}\!\to\!\mathbb{R}^{d^{\prime}}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d^{\prime}\!\ll d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0.108em">≪</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d^{\prime}\!\ll d</annotation></semantics></math> to run the
generative model in latent space.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> compresses a <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>100M ConvNeXt into a
much smaller latent and performs diffusion in that space, mitigating the curse of dimensionality.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">It has been noted that well-structured latents often admit semantic arithmetic:
interpolation or vector arithmetic can produce predictable changes in
behavior <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.
It is a route to controllable generation
and compositional model editing.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Conditioning: from prompts and datasets to weights.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Conditioning is where “prompt-to-model” becomes concrete.
Recent systems increasingly treat conditions as <em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">task fingerprints</em>:
a few prompts, a dataset descriptor, an image identity embedding, or an
architecture graph.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">D2NWG conditions diffusion on dataset descriptors to emit models for
multiple target domains <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soro et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Tina uses a CLIP text embedding of a user prompt to generate custom classifiers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>.
HyperDreamBooth conditions on image embeddings to produce identity
adapters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ruiz et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. A notable recent step is prompt-conditioned <em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">adapter generation</em> for
LLMs:
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> learns a map
from a small batch of unlabeled task prompts to LoRA updates, enabling
task adaptation without per-task optimization.
This strengthens the argument that conditioning need not be a handcrafted
metadata vector; it can be directly extracted from raw task prompts.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Generative Predictors for Weight Synthesis</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now summarize the predictor families and take an opinionated stance on <em id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">where each is practically strongest</em>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hypernetworks (fastest, best for personalization).</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Classical HyperNetworks generate weights from low-dimensional codes
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ha et al., 2017</a>)</cite>.
They remain the most pragmatic choice when latency matters and the
output is parameter-efficient (e.g., LoRA-like updates).
HyperDreamBooth exemplifies this: a lightweight hypernetwork generates
low-rank personalization updates in seconds <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ruiz et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
In regime (i), hypernetworks currently offer the cleanest deployment
path.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Graph-conditioned predictors (cross-architecture, but scaling-limited).</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GHN-style models predict weights from architecture graphs
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and can generalize to unseen DAGs, enabling
“zero-shot” evaluation in NAS-like workflows.
Graph MetaNetworks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lim et al., 2024</a>)</cite> push toward broader architectural
coverage.
However, scaling these predictors to modern foundation models requires
memory-safe graph representations and stronger inductive bias for
long-range dependencies.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Diffusion in weight space (expressive, currently best scaling evidence).</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Diffusion-based generators perturb real weights with noise and learn to
denoise.
D2NWG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soro et al., 2025</a>)</cite> shows dataset-conditioned generation.
Neural Network Diffusion demonstrates high-quality generation for large
vision backbones in a compressed latent space <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
More recent hybrid diffusion stacks (e.g., recurrent encoders plus
diffusion refinement) provide the strongest current evidence for
mid-scale full-weight generation.
We therefore view diffusion (particularly latent or hybrid diffusion) as
the most promising direction for regime (ii), where distributional
coverage and fidelity dominate.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Normalizing flows (one-step sampling, promising but less mature).</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Flow-matching approaches such as FLoWN offer invertible, one-step
sampling of weights <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Saragih et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, with potential advantages in
controllability and likelihood-based evaluation.
Their maturity and scale are currently behind diffusion,
but they remain attractive where low-latency conditional sampling is
critical.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hybrid stacks.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Hybrid predictors explicitly implement a curriculum:
first model global inter-layer structure, then refine local details.
RPG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> is emblematic: a recurrent proto-encoder captures long-range
dependencies, and diffusion fills token-level detail
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We note that RPG represents a milestone by efficiently synthesizing entire ConvNeXts or ViTs (up to  200M weights) in a single GPU pass - the first approach to go beyond toy 10M-parameter models to competitive 100M+ parameters, generated on commodity hardware. RPG-produced ConvNeXt-L matches conventional training within a few tenths of a percent on ImageNet. While other diffusion-based approaches <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soro et al., 2025</a>)</cite> addressed scaling through modular generation, they often missed inter-block correlations, yielding suboptimal results.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Training Strategies and Collapse Avoidance</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Training weight generators differs from standard generative modeling in
two ways: (i) the data distribution is highly multi-modal (many tasks,
architectures, and training recipes), and (ii) naive maximum-likelihood
can collapse to memorization of a few basins.
Practical training therefore relies on various stabilization techniques.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Augmentation and regularization.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Basic noise injection and dropout over tokens mitigate memorization.
MixUp-in-weight-space enlarges distributional support and improves
generalization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shamsian et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Contrastive objectives can encourage invariance to permutations and
training artifacts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.
For INR generators, rendering-based fidelity losses (e.g., IoU penalties)
provide functional supervision beyond raw weight error
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Erkoç et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Curriculum learning.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Practical curricula include shorter diffusion chains, smaller token
sets, and progressively increasing context length, as in RPG
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
Conceptually, this corresponds to learning global structure first (easy)
and token-level detail later (hard), matching the hierarchical
dependence structure suggested by Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Theoretical Foundation of Weight Space Geometry: Why Feasible, Yet Non-Trivial ‣ Position: Weight Space Should Be a First-Class Generative AI Modality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Diverse model zoos and task coverage.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Diverse corpora reduce collapse by forcing the generator to explain
multiple basins.
D2NWG explicitly trains on heterogeneous checkpoint zoos
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soro et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles et al., 2022</a>)</cite> scale supervision dramatically, training on
tens of millions of checkpoints to learn generative update rules.
SANE aggregates multiple public model zoos and achieves strong zero-shot
viability without overfitting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schürholt et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5 </span>Evaluation Metrics: Beyond One Simple Accuracy</h3>

<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A core critique of early weight-generation papers is that they over-index
on task accuracy and under-specify how to evaluate generalization,
novelty, and reliability.
Evaluation must therefore be multi-axis, reflecting the fact that many
distinct weights can yield similar accuracy but differ sharply in
robustness, calibration, privacy risk, or mergeability.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Three-Axis Framework.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We believe that any viable benchmark should report three axes as naturally induced by Fig. <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction and Statement of Position ‣ Position: Weight Space Should Be a First-Class Generative AI Modality" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>: (A) <span id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">within-architecture generation</span>, where we must test against nearest-neighbor retrieval, aligned interpolation, and model soups; (B) <span id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">conditional adaptation</span>, where prompt-, dataset-, or user-conditioned generators are compared against PEFT/fine-tuning under matched wall-clock and memory budgets; and (C) <span id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">cross-architecture generation</span>, where graph-conditioned generators are evaluated on held-out architecture families and unseen tensor schemas. Then, along each axis, evaluation should include downstream performance, generation cost, diversity and ensemble gain, calibration, robustness, memorization, provenance, and safety.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Task performance and adaptation efficiency.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Accuracy (or BLEU / RL return) remains primary, but should be reported
alongside adaptation cost: GPU-hours, wall-clock generation time, and
memory footprint.
For example, RPG-generated ConvNeXt-L matches fully trained ImageNet
accuracy in under 90 seconds <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
For personalization, <em id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">time-to-personalize</em> is often the key metric.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Novelty vs. interpolation baselines.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A generator is considered novel only if it outperforms strong
baselines such as aligned interpolation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ainsworth et al., 2023</a>)</cite> or model soups <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wortsman et al., 2022</a>)</cite> at comparable
distance. This concern is not hypothetical: recent diagnostic work reports that
several representative weight generators produce replicas or simple
interpolations of training checkpoints, and fail to outperform simple
noise or ensemble baselines when novelty and performance are required jointly
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zeng et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Representation similarity measures such as CKA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kornblith et al., 2019</a>)</cite>
help detect trivial memorization, while spectral signatures (e.g., singular
value distributions) test whether the generator matches the geometry of trained solutions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Diversity and mode coverage.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since many solutions exist, generators should be evaluated for ensemble
utility and mode coverage.
Pairwise disagreement, ensemble gains, and performance variance across
samples quantify whether the generator populates multiple basins.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Robustness, calibration, and trust metrics.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS5.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Even within connected basins, models differ in robustness and
calibration.
Standard tools include NLL under corruption, ECE, and adversarial or
stress-test evaluation.
Model soups demonstrate that weight averaging can improve robustness
without extra inference cost <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wortsman et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, motivating
evaluation against such strong non-generative baselines.
Depending on deployment, evaluation should extend to fairness and safety
benchmarks such as trust and privacy assessment suites
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2023a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Applications Enabled by Weight Generators</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Instant Personalization</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Weight generation has revolutionized model personalization across domains by
amortizing adaptation into a single forward pass.
In visual generation, HyperDreamBooth <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ruiz et al., 2024</a>)</cite>
dramatically accelerates subject-specific adaptation by producing weight
updates in one pass, achieving personalization in <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>20 seconds
(<math id="S4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="25\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>25</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">25\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster than DreamBooth <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ruiz et al., 2023</a>)</cite>) while
preserving base-model knowledge and style diversity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond images, Tina <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> enables <em id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">text-to-model</em>
generation, instantiating task-specific classifiers directly from textual
descriptions using a single diffusion model.
D2NWG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Soro et al., 2025</a>)</cite> further generalizes this paradigm to
dataset-conditioned full weight synthesis, matching standard transfer
learning accuracy while improving few-shot performance by <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∼</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sim</annotation></semantics></math>6%, and
extending to language models where it enhances LLaMA’s mathematical
reasoning.
Most recently, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> enable on-the-fly task adaptation of LLMs: a user simply provides a description of a new task (e.g. a specific style of Q&amp;A or a new programming API), and the system drops in a generated LoRA adapter that immediately makes the LLM perform well on that task. They demonstrated strong zero-shot generalization to tasks unseen during generator training, such as reasoning puzzles and multimodal queries, with performance even above that of standard fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Model Fusion and Editing</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Generative weight models provide new tools for combining knowledge from multiple models or domains.
Traditional model fusion techniques typically require models to be trained on related data and carefully aligned in a shared coordinate frame, and even then produce only crude combinations that may underperform on complex tasks.
In contrast, generative approaches can learn a weight-space distribution or <em id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">manifold</em> that encompasses diverse domains, enabling smooth interpolation or conditional sampling.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For example, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peebles et al., 2022</a>)</cite> showed that training a generative model on checkpoints from both image classification and language tasks yields latent interpolations that produce models with mixed characteristics, hinting at cross-domain fusion through learned manifolds.
Recent work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dravid et al., 2024</a>)</cite> on interpreting the weight space of customized diffusion models demonstrates this phenomenon at scale: by populating a large dataset of fine-tuned diffusion checkpoints and projecting them into a low-dimensional subspace, they found that navigating within this learned subspace can generate new diffusion models encoding novel identities, and that linear directions in this space correspond to semantic edits (e.g., adding visual attributes) in the resulting models.
This empirical evidence suggests that fine-tuned model weights behave as an interpretable meta-latent space where interpolation and controlled traversal produce meaningful, high-performing models.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Efficient Neural Architecture Search</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Weight generation transforms Neural Architecture Search (NAS) by eliminating costly training of candidate architectures. By training hypernetworks that map architectures to performant weights <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brock et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, researchers can instantly predict weights for unseen architectures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">GHN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, trained on one million neural nets, can predict on unseen and diverse networks, including all 24 million weights of a ResNet-50 in one forward pass, achieving 50% ImageNet top-5 accuracy and 60% CIFAR-10 top-1 without any SGD. These predicted weights serve as excellent initializations that can be quickly fine-tuned. Recent advances like GHN-3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knyazev et al., 2023</a>)</cite> use Transformer-based hypernetworks to predict weights that outperform standard one-epoch SGD training, making “zero-shot” NAS feasible for exploring ultra-large design spaces.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>On-Device Learning</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Weight-generation methods also have important implications for on-device learning. By performing learning in a lightweight hypernetwork and deploying only its generated weights, the device does not undergo heavy training, and sensitive user data never leave the device. Several systems demonstrate its effectiveness. SecDOOD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025</a>)</cite> employs a cloud-based hypernetwork for video OOD detection on IoT devices, mapping encrypted feature summaries to specialized model weights without exposing raw data. In federated learning, pFedHN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shamsian et al., 2021</a>)</cite> utilizes a global hypernetwork to generate personalized models for each client, sharing only hypernetwork parameters while significantly outperforming traditional federated averaging and generalizing better to new clients.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>The Next Frontier: Scaling Up Weight Generation to Foundation Models?</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While synthesizing arbitrary trillion-parameter models end-to-end remains an open challenge, conditional weight generation has recently scaled far beyond toy settings and is advancing rapidly. It now operates on nontrivial large backbones, where deployment cost, adaptation latency, and repeated fine-tuning overhead are major practical bottlenecks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The clearest evidence to date is <span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">HY-WU</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team and others, 2026</a>)</cite>, which
recasts conditional weight generation as a <em id="S5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">functional neural
memory</em>: instead of repeatedly overwriting a shared parameter vector, a
generator synthesizes instance-conditioned LoRA updates on the fly and
injects them into a frozen backbone without test-time optimization.
